segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then is the advantage of the Jew, or what is the benefit of circumcision?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Much in every way. To begin with, they were entrusted with the oracles of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What if some were unfaithful? Will their unfaithfulness nullify the faithfulness of God?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By no means! Let God be true and every person a liar, as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “So that you may be vindicated in your words and prevail when you are judged.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if our unrighteousness brings out the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unrighteous for inflicting wrath? I am speaking in a human way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By no means! For then how will God judge the world?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if through my lie the truth of God has abounded to his glory, why am I too still being judged as a sinner?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And why not say, as we are slanderously reported and as some claim that we say, “Let us do evil so that good may come”? Their condemnation is just.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then? Are we any better off? Not at all, for we have already charged that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “There is no one righteous, not even one;

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: there is no one who understands, no one who seeks God.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: All have turned aside; together they have become worthless. There is no one who does good, not even one.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: Their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they practice deceit. The venom of asps is under their lips,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: and their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: Their feet are swift to shed blood;

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: ruin and misery are in their paths,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: and the way of peace they have not known.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: There is no fear of God before their eyes.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are within the law, so that every mouth may be shut and the whole world become answerable to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For by works of the law no human being will be justified before him, since through the law comes the knowledge of sin.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been disclosed, attested by the Law and the Prophets,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: whom God put forward as a place of atonement, through faith, by his blood. This was to show his righteousness, because he had passed over the sins committed beforehand

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in God’s forbearance; it was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he himself is just and justifies the one who has faith in Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Where then is boasting? It has been shut out. Through what kind of law? A law of works? No, but through a law of faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also the God of Gentiles? Yes, of Gentiles also,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: since God is one, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do we then nullify the law through faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.

notes.note: Verses 2-3 play on one Greek root four times: 'entrusted', 'were unfaithful', 'unfaithfulness' and 'faithfulness' are all forms of the word elsewhere translated 'faith' or 'believe'. Here the noun plainly means God's reliability in keeping his word, not anyone's belief, so 'faithfulness' is used, as in most modern translations.

Greek has one word-family where English has two: 'righteous' and 'just', 'righteousness' and 'justice', 'justify' and 'vindicate' all render the same root. In this quotation God is shown to be in the right, so 'vindicated' is used; elsewhere in the chapter the same verb is 'justify', and 'just' in verse 26 is the word translated 'righteous' in verse 10. Translations from Latin and most other languages use their single word for 'justice' throughout, and some scholars prefer 'justice' or 'covenant faithfulness' for the noun in English.

The Greek form can be passive ('when you are judged') or middle ('when you go to law'). The Hebrew of Psalm 51:4 reads 'when you judge'. Paul quotes the Greek version, which pictures God as a party in a dispute who wins his case.

The verb form is rare and its sense here is disputed. Most take it as 'Do we Jews have an advantage?'; others read it as passive, 'Are we at a disadvantage?', or as 'Are we making excuses?'. The reply can also be read as 'Not altogether' instead of 'Not at all'.

notes.phrase: There is no one righteous, not even one
notes.note: Verses 10-18 are a chain of Scripture passages quoted from the Greek version and joined as one indictment: Psalm 14:1-3 (also Psalm 53), Psalm 5:9, Psalm 140:3, Psalm 10:7, Isaiah 59:7-8 and Psalm 36:1. Stringing texts together in this way was an established Jewish practice.

Literally 'all flesh will not be justified', a Semitic idiom meaning 'no one at all'. Paul is echoing Psalm 143:2. Elsewhere this translation keeps 'flesh' for the Greek word; in this idiom it simply means humanity.

Traditionally understood as deeds done in obedience to the law of Moses in general, viewed as a way of gaining standing with God. Many recent scholars think the phrase refers especially to the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles, such as circumcision, food laws and the sabbath. The question remains disputed, and the rendering is left as open as the Greek.

The Greek is literally 'faith of Jesus Christ' and can mean either faith directed toward Christ or Christ's own faithfulness, that is, his obedience unto death. 'Faith in Jesus Christ' is the traditional and still majority reading; 'the faithfulness of Jesus Christ' has substantial scholarly support, and would make 'for all who believe' less repetitive.

In the Greek Old Testament this word is the name of the gold cover of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16); Hebrews 9:5 uses it in that sense. The rendering lets that allusion be heard. Whether Paul means the ark's cover, 'propitiation' (turning away wrath) or 'expiation' (removing sin) is a long-running dispute.

The older tradition joined the two phrases as 'faith in his blood'. Most interpreters now connect 'by his blood' with 'place of atonement', since Paul nowhere else speaks of faith in blood. Some also take 'through faith' here as 'through faithfulness', whether God's or Christ's.

notes.phrase: the one who has faith in Jesus
notes.note: Literally 'the one from faith of Jesus'. As in verse 22, the phrase may instead mean 'the one who lives out of the faithfulness of Jesus'. The rendering follows the majority reading.

The word is the one used throughout the chapter for the law of Moses. Many translations render it 'principle' here, taking Paul to be playing on the word. Others think he still means the Mosaic law, seen either as demanding works or as calling for faith. 'Law' is kept so the reader sees the same word.

candidates.reason: Recurs constantly in Paul with shifting reference (Mosaic law, Scripture, 'principle'), and capitalisation and the 'principle' option need one policy.
A favourite Pauline verb rendered variously as nullify, abolish, destroy or make void; readers lose the thread if it varies without reason.
The choice between 'Gentiles' and 'nations' recurs across the whole New Testament and affects how the Jew/non-Jew contrast reads.
'Redemption' is now largely religious jargon, while the Greek evoked release by ransom; a single decision is needed across Paul, Hebrews and Luke.
Central to Romans 4 ('counted/credited/reckoned') and frequent elsewhere in the sense 'consider'; the senses need fixed renderings.
